Lung cancer is a cancer that forms in tissues of the lung, usually in the cells lining air passages. The two main types are small cell lung cancer and non-small cell lung cancer.
Incidence rate among all races is 82.1 per 100,000 men per year and 52.3 per 100,000 women per year.
African-American males have the highest incidence of lung cancer at 113.9 per 100,000 persons per year.
2.1 million cases of lung cancer worldwide, with 1.8 million deaths.
Approximately 541,000 Americans living today have been diagnosed with lung cancer during their lifetime.
Direct medical cost for treatment of lung cancer is estimated at approximately $13.4 billion annually.
Lost productivity due to early death from lung cancer is estimated to cost $36.1 billion annually.
Lung cancer is the second most common cancer and the leading cause of cancer-related death in the United States in both men and women.
1 in 14 men and women will be diagnosed with lung cancer during their lifetime.
In the last decade, death rates from lung cancer among men have begun to decline, but lung cancer recently surpassed breast cancer as the most common fatal cancer among women.
Smoking is directly linked to lung cancer in 90% of cases in women and 79% of cases in men. A clinical rule can be used to determine the risk of cancer in smokers.

Exposures to second-hand smoke, asbestos, radon, or ionizing radiation and preexisting nonmalignant pulmonary diseases, such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, and tuberculosis are also associated with increased lung cancer rates.

A recent analysis of 14 case control studies with a total of over 28,000 participants demonstrated increased risk of lung cancer with occupational benzene exposure, which varied with exposure dose and duration.
Lung cancer is broadly categorized as small cell carcinoma or non-small cell carcinoma.
Light microscopy is used to differentiate lung cancer further into four major and several minor histologic classes.
The major histologic classes are adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, small cell carcinoma, and large cell carcinoma.
Minor histologic classes include adenosquamous carcinoma, carcinoid, and bronchial gland carcinoma.
Adenocarcinoma recently surpassed squamous cell carcinoma as the most common type of lung carcinoma.
USPSTF now recommends screening for lung cancer in high risk adults (age 50-80 years, 20 pack years of smoking, and still smoking or quit within 15 years).
For all individuals, smoking cessation should be strongly encouraged to decrease the risk of lung cancer. B

Chest radiography and sputum cytology are not effective screening tools for lung cancer. The former was confirmed by the PLCO trial, which found no impact on lung cancer mortality over 4 years in those randomized to CXR.

Low dose spiral chest CT detects lung cancer earlier in high-risk patients. The 3 year results for the DANTE study which randomized over 2800 smokers to CT screening or no screening resulted in a greater number of detected cancers in the screened group (4.7% vs 2.8%) and more operable cancers, but no difference in mortality. Early results from the NELSON trial found that CT had a 36% positive predictive value after the first round of screening, but at a cost of many biopsies and significant radiation exposure.

Most recently, the National Lung Cancer Screening Trial reported results from an RCT that enrolled 53,454 persons age 55 to 74 years with at least 30 pack years smoking and who were currently smoking or had quit within 15 years. Patients were followed for 5 years, and the screened group had lower lung-cancer-specific mortality (249 vs 309 deaths/100,000 person-years, p = 0.004) and lower all-cause mortality (1877 vs 2000 deaths, p = 0.02). The NNS over the 5 year study period is 320. However, false positives are common, requiring additional surveillance and often biopsy or even surgery. Thus, harms are potentially quite substantial for patients participating in a screening program.

The USPSTF now recommends screening with low dose CT for high risk smokers (age 50-80 years, 20 pack years, and still smoking or quit within 15 years). However, there is concern that screening may cause overdiagnosis and unnecessary anxiety, radiation exposure, and expense.
Recent systematic reviews including the major screening trials (NELSON and NLST) estimate the rate of overdiagnosis at between 8% and 20%.

A cost-effectiveness analysis performed after the Task Force recommendation was released concluded that screening was most cost-effective in current smokers, among persons aged 60 to 69 years, and in those at the highest two quintiles of lung cancer risk.
Among the screen-detected nodules, predictors of malignancy include female sex, upper lobe nodules, spiculation, and larger nodule size.

The ACS, ACCP, NCCN, and ASCO recommend that screening be offered to high risk patients, but express concerns about potential harms if patients are not appropriately selected. There is ACCP guidance published on the components required for effective screening programs to ensure quality and governance.

A review of the American College of Radiology database on over one million of the population who have undergone screening demonstrated a cancer detection rate of only 0.56%, poor adherence to proposed test schedule at 22% and particularly poor adherence in smokers who were the most at risk cohort.

In one recent series initial screening led to additional imaging in 40% of patients in the real world situation which does raise questions about cost-effectiveness. However, a subsequent larger study found rates of imaging in a community sample were lower than in the NLST, although rates of some invasive procedures were higher. Cost-effectiveness of screening depends on effectiveness of individual programs. A clinical rule can assist in decision-making by identifying patients at greater risk who are more likely to have a favorable benefit-harm ratio.

Review of US population of almost 10,000 screened patients highlighted that almost 16% of patients screened with low dose CT had abnormal scans, with a third of patients requiring additional imaging, 2.8% receiving invasive investigations and of those one third had complications. The overall diagnostic rate for cancer was low and caution should be applied in weighing up the benefit of screening.
The Liverpool Lung Project has developed an accurate risk prediction model that is publicly available here. It has been prospectively validated.

2020 saw publication of final results of NELSON, the Dutch screening trial of over 15,000 people using low dose CT. NELSON was notable for gradually spacing out screening intervals from 1 to 1.5 to 2 years without loss of benefit.. A meta-analysis including the NLST and NELSON results reached the same conclusion that lung cancer mortality is reduced but not overall mortality using low dose CT screening in high risk populations. The absolute reduction in lung cancer is low (0.4%) with 8% participants 'overdiagnosed'.

A review that modeled alternative criteria for selection for lung cancer screening suggests it may be possible to improve the benefit to risk ratio with criteria focusing on the higher risk individuals in terms of age and smoking history. This approach could improve sensitivity of screening from 78 to 91% with an even greater increase in the specifically high risk cohort of racial and ethnic minorities.
A systematic review concluded that while AI over-reading of imaging may increase sensitivity of screening CT, it also increases false positives and the need for further surveillance.
For all individuals, smoking cessation should be strongly encouraged to decrease the risk of lung cancer.
For lung cancer prevention, smokers should be offered nicotine replacement therapy, buproprion (Wellbutrin), nortiptyline (Pamelor), and counseling for smoking cessation.
There is currently no evidence to support recommending vitamins A, C, E, beta-carotene, selenium, or retinol to prevent lung cancer.

A Cochrane review of 51 studies and more than 1.6 million participants concluded there was insufficient and conflicting evidence to support a benefit for green tea consumption in primary prevention of lung cancer.

Lung cancer patients who smoke should be strongly encouraged to stop smoking. A review of outcomes in NCSLC comparing smokers to non-smokers found similar rates of 12 month progression free survival and all cause mortality, but with survival significantly worse at 5 and 10 years for the continuing smokers.

Transthoracic needle aspiration is recommended in patients with peripheral lung tumors who are not surgical candidates. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Other signs of malignancy from primary tumor

list.listitem: Non-small cell carcinoma is categorized using the TNM (tumor-node-metastases) staging system.

Small cell carcinoma, previously categorized as limited or extensive stage disease, is now staged also on TNM system since introduction of updated TNM version 7 in 2012 (current version is now TNMv8).
Common manifestations of a primary tumor include chest or rib pain, cough, dyspnea, and hemoptysis.

Approximately 40% of patients present with signs and symptoms of intrathoracic spread, including chest wall invasion, esophageal symptoms, Horner syndrome, Pancoast's tumor, phrenic nerve paralysis, recurrent laryngeal nerve paralysis, pleural effusions, and superior vena cava syndrome.

About one-third of patients present with signs and symptoms of extrathoracic spread, including nonspecific signs such as fatigue, weight loss, and decreased appetite as well as bone pain, fracture, elevated alkaline phosphatase, confusion, focal neurologic deficits, headache, seizures, nausea, vomiting, or palpable lymphadenopathy.

A smaller percentage of patients present with symptoms related to paraneoplastic syndromes such as hypercalcemia, SIADH, Cushing's syndrome, digital clubbing, hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthorpathy, Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, peripheral neuropathy, and cortical cerebellar degeneration.
All patients with known or suspected lung cancer should undergo a thorough history, physical examination, and standard laboratory tests as a screen for metastatic disease.
A history of dyspnea, chest or rib pain, fatigue, hemoptysis, weight loss, loss of appetite, or fatigue should raise suspicion for lung cancer.
The presence of finger clubbing on physical exam has a low sensitivity but a high specificity for pulmonary disease.

Approximately 10% of lung cancers are detected on chest radiographs in asymptomatic patients. In patients with pleural effusion, CA 15-3, CA 125, CA 19-9, and CYFRA 21-1 antigens suggest malignancy. The most accurate combination was CA 125 + CA 19-9 (LR+ 47, LR− 0.05).

A systematic review found two good quality studies of CXR for the diagnosis of lung cancer, and found sensitivities of 77% to 80%. Patients with negative CXR but at high clinical risk should have further imaging.

A tissue diagnosis may be obtained through a variety of techniques, including sputum cytology, thoracentesis, excisional biopsy of an accessible node, flexible bronchoscopy with or without transbronchial needle aspiration, transthoracic needle aspiration, and video-assisted thoracoscopy or thoracotomy.
Patients undergoing mediastinal staging for lung cancer should receive chest computed tomography plus positron emission tomography.

Pulmonary function testing, including forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) and carbon monoxide diffusion in the lung (DLCO) measurement, is a helpful predictor of morbidity and mortality in patients undergoing lung resection.

Non-small cell lung cancer: NCCN guidelines recommend pathology review, CT chest and upper abdomen including adrenals, CBC, platelets, chemistry profile for initial evaluation of patients with non-small cell lung cancer. For patients in whom curative therapy options are being considered, staging should include a PET scan to better define extent of disease and exclude occult metastases.

Small cell lung cancer: NCCN Guidelines recommend pathology review, chest/liver/adrenal CT, CBC, platelets, electrolytes, LFTs, calcium, LDH, BUN, creatinine for initial evaluation. CXR and PET scan are optional, as is bone scan if PET scan has been obtained. Head MRI is also recommended, with CT as an alternative.

With the increasing therapeutic options deriving from actionable mutations, it should now be standard that pathology reporting of lung cancers includes screening for the common mutations and for PDL1.
Clinical decision rules have been developed to predict the prognosis of patients with terminal lung cancer and non-small cell lung cancer.
The Liverpool Lung Project has developed an accurate risk prediction model that is publicly available here. It has been prospectively validated.
A clinical rule has also been developed to predict an individual's risk of developing lung cancer.
A clinical rule can determine the risk of lung cancer to aid in screening decisions.

In patients with apparent early non-small cell carcinomas who are surgical candidates, bronchoscopy with endobronchial ultrasound (EBUS)-directed biopsy is used commonly due to its high diagnostic accuracy.

In patients with presumed small cell or metastatic non-small cell carcinomas, the diagnosis should be made by using the most convenient and least invasive method available, such as thoracentesis of a pleural effusion, excisional biopsy of an accessible node, bronchoscopy, or transthoracic needle aspiration.
Transthoracic needle aspiration is recommended in patients with peripheral lung tumors who are not surgical candidates.

After establishing a tissue diagnosis, a metastatic evaluation and staging classification should be performed to determine the presence of metastasis and to identify surgical resection candidates. Initial evaluation includes a thorough history and physical exam, lab evaluation, and chest and upper abdomen CT scans plus PET scan.

If mediastinum appears normal, perform mediastinoscopy and thoracotomy. If mediastinal spread is suspected, choose one of the following based on clinical presentation: Bronchoscopy with or without transbronchial needle aspiration Endobronchial ultrasonography: guided transbronchial needle aspiration Transthoracic needle aspiration Video-assisted thoracoscopy Mediastinoscopy
After a metastatic evaluation is complete, the staging classification can be determined based on the type of tumor identified and the presence or absence of metastatic disease.
A final component of the diagnostic assessment of patients with lung cancer is a functional evaluation, including evaluation of performance and pulmonary status.
Surgery is the treatment of choice for patients with local or only locally advanced non-small cell carcinoma (Stage I through Stage IIIA). B
Treatment for unresectable non-small cell carcinoma may involve radiotherapy and chemotherapy. C
Chemotherapy, combined with radiotherapy in limited disease, is the mainstay of treatment for small cell carcinoma. C
Targeted therapy for NSCLC directed against specific mutations identified within the tumours is highly effective. B
There is no evidence that elemene, a Chinese herb, is effective for lung cancer treatment. Many of the trials reported as randomized were actually non-randomized clinical trials.

Breathing training, walking aids, neuro-electrical muscular stimulation and chest wall vibration are all helpful for patients with advanced lung cancer and breathlessness.There is also evidence for benefit from exercise programs following surgery.
Nursing interventions to reduce breathlessness are effective.

listitem.strong: Treatment of Small Cell Lung Cancer

list.listitem: The mainstay of drug therapy for small cell lung cancer is platinum-based combination chemotherapy. There was a trend toward better 3 year survival with earlier initiation of radiotherapy (within 30 days of the start of chemotherapy) but it lacked statistical significance.
Consider lobectomy with mediastinal dissection in patients with Stage I to IIA SCLC.

The addition of chest radiotherapy in patients responding to primary chemotherapy has been shown to improve overall survival in both limited and extensive stage disease as has the addition of prophylactic cranial radiotherapy.
Lobectomy and mediastinal lymph node dissection or sampling are an option for patients with clinical state T1-2,N0 small cell lung cancer.
Atezolizumab has also shown a small benefit in both progression free survival and median survival when added to standard chemotherapy in metastatic small cell lung cancer.
Immunotherapy with durvalumab after concurrent chemoradiotherapy in limited stage small cell lung cancer improved median survival in a large study from 33.4 to 55.9 months.
Second-line therapies include lurbinectidin and tarlatamab.
Anti-coagulation: A systematic review of 5 RCTs found no evidence of mortality benefit for anticoagulation in patients with lung cancer.
Antitussives: Studies of cough in patients with lung cancer are of poor quality. There is some evidence of benefit for opiates, and possibly brachytherapy and photodynamic therapy.
Palliative lower dose radiotherapy provides effective symptom control and may prolong survival in selected patients.

listitem.strong: Treatment of Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer (NSCLC)

list.listitem: Surgery is the treatment of choice for patients with local or only locally advanced non-small cell carcinoma (Stage I through Stage IIIA). B
A trial randomized 697 patients with T1aN0 (tumor size <= 2 cm) to sublobar versus lobar resection. They concluded that sublobar resection was non-inferior to lobar resection after 5 years.

A meta-analysis identified 5 RCTs with 2035 patients comparing sublobar vs lobar resection for patients with early stage NSCLC <= 2 cm in diabeter, and found that sublobar was non-inferior. Relative risk of 5 year survival was the same between groups (RR 1.02 favoring sublobar, 95% CI 0.99 to 1.05).

Evidence from a meta-analysis suggests that the benefit of adjuvant chemotherapy in NSCLC is in patients with nodal involvement or tumour >4 cm, and even in these groups the benefits of adjuvant chemotherapy is limited to increased 5 year survival from 41% to 45% with significant risk of toxicity.

In patients who have had surgical resection of tumours with EGFR sensitising mutations there is early evidence of reduced recurrence with adjuvant use of osimertinib but mature survival data is awaited.

A similar trial using adjuvant osimertinib after primary chemoradiotherapy in inoperable EGFR mutated NSCLC has also demonstrated benefit in progression free survival but mature data on survival is awaited.
Recent Cochrane reviews demonstrate no evidence of survival benefit for prophylactic anticoagulation in patients without evidence of thrombus.

Treatment for unresectable non-small cell carcinoma may involve radiotherapy and chemotherapy. A systematic review found that survival was improved for supportive care plus chemotherapy compared with supportive care alone. A second chemotherapy drug may increase tumor response, but less so with a third drug.
Similarly adding pembrolizumab to neoadjuvant chemotherapy and adding it adjuvantly improved event free survival and with evidence of overall survival benefit at 3 years from 64 to 71%.
A further trial of neoadjuvant chemotherapy with or without nivolumab immunotherapy pre-operatively confirmed a significant 5 year survival benefit in the immunotherapy group 65 vs 55%.

Another systematic review found that external beam radiation is more effective than endobronchial brachytherapy for patients with inoperable non-small cell lung cancer, but the value of combining these therapies is unknown.

Radiotherapy is the treatment of choice for medically inoperable patients with early stage non-small cell lung cancer and offers potentially curative therapy for those unfit for surgery. Short course high biological dose radiation delivered as stereotactic therapy (SBRT) is an evolving option for treatment of peripheral early stage tumours with outcomes suggesting this may offer an alternative to surgery in some patients. Analysis of the National Cancer Database has shown that in medically inoperable NSCLC, SBRT offers better survival than no treatment. A recent meta-analysis including almost 18,000 patients with inoperable early stage NSCLC demonstrated better local control and overall survival with the use of stereotactic radiotherapy as compared to conventional radiotherapy.

Radical dose, potentially curative radiation treatment, is the treatment of choice in locally advanced NSCLC. In fit patients, outcomes are improved with addition of systemic therapy. If systemic therapy is administered concurrently this is more effective, though potentially more toxic, than given sequentially.

Targeted therapy for NSCLC directed against specific mutations identified within the tumours has opened up a huge therapeutic potential currently in development. In the patient population with the specific anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) genetic translocation, an RCT demonstrated response rate of 74% compared to standard chemotherapy response rate of 45%. There have been a number of trials addressing the efficacy of immunotherapy agents in second line treatment of NSCLC, randomising against the standard treatment docetaxel. All have shown significant increases in overall survival indicating a whole new option of treatment.

A clinical trial identified 275 patients with ALK positive NSCLC and randomized them to one of two ALK inhibitors, brigatinib or crizotinib. The 12 month median progression free survival was higher with brigatinib (67% vs 43%, p <0.001, NNT = 4).With the option now of a third generation agent targetting ALK translocation, response rate and progression free survival were improved with lorlatinib compared to crizotinib and this was especially true in patients with brain disease. The percentage alive without disease progression at 12 months was 78% with loraltinib and only 39% with crizotinimb (HR 0.28, 95% CI 0.19-0.41).

Adagrasib is a KRASG12C inhibitor. In a prospective cohort, 116 patients who had already been treated with platinum based chemotherapy and anti-programmed death 1 or ligand 1 therapy were treated with adagrasib; 43% had a response with a median duration of 8 months.

An RCT enrolled 305 patients with advanced, previously untreated NSCLC who expressed a high level of PD-L1 on the cancer cells. The trial compared pembrolizumab (a monoclonal antibody) with platinum-based chemotherapy. Median progression-free survival favored the pembrolizumab group (10.3 vs 6.0 months, p <0.001), with 6 month survival of 80% vs 72%, p = 0.005, NNT = 13). The therapy was also better tolerated.

A study randomized 797 participants with early stage (II, IIIA or IIIE) NSCLC to pembrolizumab or placebo, followed by resection. Overall survival at 24 months was slightly higher in the pembrolizumab group (80.9% vs 77.6%, p = 0.02) as was 24 month event free survival (62.4% vs 40.6%, p < 0.001).

A study randomized 559 patients with metastatic squamous NSCLC to standard chemotherapy + pembrolizumab or standard chemotherapy + placebo. At a median of 7.8 months, overall survival was higher in the combination therapy group (15.9 months vs 11.3 months, p <0.001), while progression free survival was also somewhat higher (6.4 vs 4.8 months, p <0.001).

This finding of enhanced overall survival with the addition of immunotherapy to first line chemotherapy in advanced NSCLC has now been replicated across a number of trials using different immunotherapy agents.
With the agent atezolizumab the benefit has been demonstrated regardless of PDL1 status.

A trial comparing nivolumab plus ipilimumab with standard chemotherapy in patients with at least 1% PD-L1 expression and advanced stage NSCLC found slightly longer survival with combination therapy (17.1 months vs 14.9 months with chemotherapy). Further studies combining PD1 and CTLA4 inhibition also show promising results, though with an increased risk of toxicity with combination immunotherapy.

A study of patients with stage IB to IIIA resectable non-small cell lung cancer randomized 358 patients to platinum-based chemotherapy alone or nivolumab with chemotherapy. Event free survival was longer with combination therapy (32 vs 21 months, p = 0.005) as was the number of patients with a complete pathologic response (24% vs 2%, p < 0.001, NNT = 5). Adverse events were similar between groups. The final follow-up reported better overall survival found in the nivolumab group (HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.52 to 0.998). At 68 months, 5 year overall survival was higher (65% vs 55%, NNT = 10).

A study gave patients with resectable stage IIa to IIIb NSCLC nivolumab perioperatively plus neoadjuvant chemotherapy or neoadjuvant chemotherapy alone. Event free survival was more common with perioperative nivolumab at median 25 month follow-up (70% vs 50%, HR 0.58, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.81).

A trial of 86 patients with resectable Stage III NSCLC randomized them to neoadjuvant nivolumab + platinum-based chemotherapy or chemotherapy alone. The group receiving nivolumab were more likely to undergo surgery and had improved progression free survival at 24 months (67% vs 41%, HR 0.47, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.88, NNT = 4).

Immunotherapy has now been approved for use in locally advanced disease following the PACIFIC trial with 709 patients treated with maintenance durvalumab following chemoradiation for stage III NSCLC. Median survival was 28.3 months in the treatent arm compared to 10.2 months in the control arm.

A study randomized 802 patients with resectable Stage II to IIIB NSCLC to platinum-based chemotherapy plus durvalumab or placebo. Event-free survival at 24 months (no disease progression, recurrence, or death) was more likely with durvalumab (63.3% vs 52.4%, p < 0.05, NNT = 10). While named as a secondary endpoint, overall survival was not reported separately.

The introduction of immunotherapy agents has produced a raft of potential new toxicities to manage ranging from endocrine to gastrointestinal to pulmonary complications. The immune related toxicities can be sudden and severe and require urgent hospitalisation with high dose steroids and supportive therapy.

An RCT identified patients with NSCLC whose disease progressed after treatment with an epidermal growth factor receptor tyrosine kinase (EGFR-TKI). They were randomized to osimertinib (an EGFR-TKI that is also selective for the T790M receptor) or platinum based therapy. Those receiving osimertinib had longer progression free survival by about 6 months (10.1 vs 4.4 months, p <0.002), and the drug was better tolerated than platinum based therapy.
Adding osimertinib to chemotherapy in EGFR mutated patients showed increased survival compared to chemotherapy alone.
Among patients with previously untreated advanced NSCLC with an EGFR mutation, those who received osimertinib had longer overall survival than those who received a comparator EGFR-TKI.

A placebo controlled RCT studied previously untreated EGFR positive patients following complete resection of NSCLC and found that at 24 months, survival was significantly higher in those randomized to osimertinib instead of placebo (90% vs 44%, p <0.001, NNT = 2).

A trial identified 682 patients with EGFR-mutated resectable stage IB to IIIA NSCLC and randomized them to osimertinib or placebo. At 5 years overall survival was higher in the treatment group (88% vs 78%, p < 0.001, NNT = 10).

In 216 patients with unresectable EGFR mutated stage III NSCLC who had already undergone chemoradiotherapy, those randomized to osimertinib were more likely to be alive and progression-free at one year (74% vs 22%). At 36 months, overall survival was 84% vs 74% but this difference was not significant (p=0.54).
In patients with NSCLC and either MET exon 14 skipping mutation of MET amplification, a cohort study found complete or partial response to the MET receptor inhibitor capmatinib.

Patients (n=308) with NSCLC and the EGFR exon 20 insertion were randomized to amivantamab plus chemotherapy or chemotherapy alone. At 18 months, progression free survival was more likely with amivantanab (31% vs 3%, p < 0.001, NNT = 3). In an interim analysis the hazard ratio for death trended in favor of treatment (HR 0.67, 95% CI 0.42-1.09).
In a cohort study of 152 patients with NSCLC and MET exon 14 skipping mutation, approximately half had a partial response with tepotinib.
In a single arm trial with 125 patients with KRAS p.G12C mutated advanced NSCLC, sotorasib resulted in a measurable response in 37% of patients including 4% with a complete response.

In those with advanced NSCLC and at least 50% PDL-1 ligand expression, the EMPOWER-Lung 1 trial found significant improvement in overall survival and progression-free survival with Cemiplimab monotherapy compared to platinum-based doublet therapy.

In a phase 1/2 trial of patients with previously treated HER2-mutant advanced or metastatic NSCLC, the HER2 selective tyrosine kinase inhibitor zontertinib elicited a clinical response in 71% with 12.9 months progression free survival.
When compared to platinum-based chemotherapy, treatment with atezolizumab resulted in significantly longer overall survival among patients with highly expressed PD-L1 NSCLC.

The latest class of new agents to emerge are targetted therapies for RET and ROS1 fusion gene mutations in Phase 2 trials, where individual drugs have demonstrated promising response rates compared to standard therapy.

In a Phase 3 trial, 212 patients with RET fusion-positive NSCLC were randomized to first-line selpercatinib versus standard platinum based chemotherapy plus or minus pembrolizumab at the treating physician's discretion. Progression-free survival was significantly greater with selpercatinib (24.8 vs 11.2 months, p < 0.001).

Malignant pleural effusion: For patients requiring pleurodesis for malignant pleural effusion, a systematic review found that talc was the sclerosant of choice, that talc did not affect mortality, and that thoracoscopic pleurodesis is the most effective technique. A study of 106 patients with malignant pleural effusion found that indwelling pleural catheter was similar to talc pleurodesis for symptom relief. The IPC patients spent less time in the hospital, were less likely to require further procedures, but were more likely to develop serious pleural infections (9.6% vs 1.9%).

Brain metastases: There is no evidence to support the effectiveness of prophylactic cranial irradiation to prevent brain metastases in patients with lung cancer. There is no evidence that chemotherapy for brain metastases is effective, based on 3 small RCTs with 192 patients.
SVC obstruction: This occurs in 10% with SCLC and 2% with NSLC. Chemotherapy and radiation are effective in most patients, but recurrence is common. Steroids have not been studied.

Breathlessness: Nursing interventions are effective. Opiates are first-line drugs, benzodiazepines are of questionable benefit and should only be used as 2nd or 3rd line drugs. Neuromuscular electrical stimulation, walking aids, breathing training, and chest wall vibration may also be effective.
Pathologic fracture: The use of bisphosphonates in patients with bone metastases has been shown to reduce the incidence of skeletal related events.

There is now increasing use of EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors in patients with mutations with demonstrable clinical benefit. However a meta-analysis of almost 30,000 patients in 89 RCTs has shown increased risk of cardiac adverse events with these drugs and a greater risk specifically with the third generation drugs, including osimertinib.
The prognosis for patients with terminal lung cancer or non-small cell lung cancer can be predicted using validated clinical rules. B

A systmatic review of 471 studies with 60,695 patients (limited to 2011 to 2021) with NSCLC found the following rates of 1 and 5 year recurrence free survival:
Stage IA: 89% 3 year, 86% 5 year survival Stage IB: 74% 3 year, 62% 5 year survival Stage I: 87% 3 year, 81% 5 year survival Stage II: 58% 3 year, 50% 5 year survival Stage III: 38% 3 year, 34% 5 year survival

Surveillance with a medical history, physical examination, and imaging study (either chest radiograph or chest CT scan) is recommended every 6 months for 2 years and then annually for patients who have been treated with curative-intent therapy. C
Untreated patients with non-small cell lung cancer live an average of 7 months.
There is evidence that early palliative care by telehealth intervention can be as effective in quality of life outcomes as in person review making this more accessible to this population.
Poor adherence to lung cancer screening over 4 years contributes to lower than expected cancer detection rate and impacts the outcomes of patients.

In one study, 1651 patients, the operative time was compared to outcomes. On multivariable analysis, operative time was associated with higher odds of any complication [odds ratio per hour, 1.37; 95% confidence interval (CI), 1.20-1.57; P <0.0001] and major complication (odds ratio per hour, 1.41; 95% CI, 1.21-1.64; P <0.0001). Operative time was also associated with longer hospital length of stay (β, 1.09; 95% CI, 1.04-1.14; P =0.001), concluding that longer operative time was associated with worse outcomes in lobectomy patients
In a study comparing smokers versus non-smokers with NSCLC, survival and mortality were significantly worse in smokers. For example, the hazard ratio for 10 year all-cause mortality was 1.77 (p=.02).
Patients with lung cancer should not be denied lung resection surgery on the basis of age alone.

In a systematic review of 52 randomized controlled trials, which included 13,660 patients, it was observed that immunotherapy alone significantly improved disease controlled rate (DCR) in early lung cancer compared to advanced lung cancer. Additionally, the improvement in objective response rate (ORR) was not the same between early and advanced disease, showing that the combination of immunotherapy with other therapies, especially immunochemotherapy, significantly improved ORR and DCR in early lung cancer. When looking at safety, immunotherapy alone or in combination with other therapies exhibited a better safety profile in early lung cancer than in advanced lung cancer. The benefits of immunotherapy in early lung cancer appeared to be better than those observed in advanced lung cancer.
